quote: In one of Frank Herbert’s Dune books, if I recall correctly, it is said that a Truthsayer gains their ability to detect lies in others by always speaking truth themselves, so that they form a relationship with the truth whose violation they can feel. It wouldn’t work
content: It would not, and the essay is right to say so, but the reason is worth stating because it bears on the book’s broader confidence in trained perception. Human lie detection runs at about 54% against a 50% chance baseline across more than two hundred studies, with no reliable improvement from experience, profession or confidence (Bond & DePaulo (2006), discussed in Book II), and the cues people believe they use (gaze aversion, fidgeting) are not diagnostic. The Truthsayer is a fantasy of a skill that the evidence says does not exist in any human, trained or not. The essay treats it as a beautiful thought about pressing oneself against reality; the more useful lesson from the same fact is that the feeling of being attuned to truth, which the Truthsayer cultivates and which the book’s later essays on the Way and the rhythm of Bayes rely on, has no measured correlation with being right.

quote: When you have arrived at your best picture of the truth, there is nothing irrational about the emotions you feel as a result of that—the emotions cannot be destroyed by truth, so they must not be irrational.
content: This is a non sequitur, and its failure is the subject of a literature. An emotion can be caused by a true belief and still misfit its object: fear of a spider that one knows to be harmless survives the knowledge, is disproportionate to the danger, and is irrational in the only sense that matters for a phobia. Emotions have correctness conditions of their own, fittingness, that are distinct from the truth of the beliefs that prompt them (D’Arms & Jacobson (2000) on the difference between an emotion being warranted by its object and being useful, moral, or caused by an accurate belief), and the appraisal theories in psychology (Lazarus, Scherer) treat the appraisal, not the fact, as what the emotion answers to. So “cannot be destroyed by truth” does not entail “not irrational”; it entails only that the irrationality is not of the belief-error kind. Book I’s annotation on Feeling Rational found the same inference there. The essay needs it in order to bless the emotions of the reductionist as beyond criticism, and the blessing is not available on these terms.

quote: Understanding that lottery tickets have negative expected utility does not mean that you give up the hope of being rich. It means that you stop wasting that hope on lottery tickets. You put the hope into your job, your school, your startup, your eBay sideline
content: The startup is the lottery ticket of the educated, and the economics literature has measured it. Entrepreneurs bear undiversified risk in their own ventures and earn, in aggregate, no premium for it over public equity (Moskowitz & Vissing-Jørgensen (2002), the “private equity premium puzzle”), and the payoff distribution for venture-backed founders is extremely skewed, with the median founder receiving little and the mean carried by a handful of outliers (Hall & Woodward (2010)). The standard explanation is that founders overweight small probabilities of large gains and derive non-pecuniary utility from the attempt, which is the explanation of lottery play. So the essay’s redirection replaces one negative-risk-adjusted gamble with another; what distinguishes them is that the second is productive for society and approved of by the author, both of which are good reasons but neither of which is the expected-utility reason the essay gives. The consistent position is either that small-probability hope is a legitimate consumption good in both cases, which the lottery buyer would accept, or that it is a waste in both, which the essay would not.
